newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Chiluba weathers storm over Zambia's flawed election.
newsitem.headline: Chiluba weathers storm over Zambia's flawed election.

text.p: Threats of sanctions, armed insurrection and foreign aid cuts against Zambia following its flawed elections last year seem to be evaporating, analysts say.

Seven political parties boycotted the November elections and the European Union cut aid after the government ordered highly controversial changes to electoral law in order to bar some candidates -- including former president Kenneth Kaunda -- from standing.
But President Frederick Chiluba appears to have weathered the storm, to emerge in an even a stronger position.

Political analysts say a divided opposition, public fatigue with acrimonious politics and a relatively stable economy have enabled Chiluba to remain firmly in the saddle despite local and international criticism of the election, which he won easily.
His opponents had banked on popular unrest and continued international economic pressure to force the government to nullify last year's poll and call a fresh ballot.
But neither form of pressure has come to much.
Analysts say public support for opposition strategies, including a continued polls boycott and an international campaign for sanctions against Zambia, appears to be dwindling.

"The opposition is only making itself irrelevant to the political process by boycotting elections," said Ngande Mwanajiti, head of the Inter African Network for Human Rights and Development (Afronet).
Civic leaders are now calling on the opposition to drop its hardline stance and reach a compromise with the government.

"If things are to go back to normal, politicians in the government and opposition political parties must embrace genuine dialogue on the various contentious issues and differences among them," said Law Association of Zambia chairman George Kunda.

However, the opposition alliance of seven parties says it will continue its boycott as well as plans to organise a civil disobedience campaign and keep up the call for economic sanctions against Zambia.
"The civil disobedience campaign is still very much on our desk, and we will carry it out," says opposition United National Independence Party (UNIP) central committee member Pickson Chitambala.
Another opposition party, Zambia Democratic Congress, has gone one step further in its continued call for an armed insurrection to unseat the government.
The party seemed headed for collapse this week after its president, former deputy minister Dean Mungomba, expelled three top officials for opposing his call to arms.
The expelled leaders insist, however, that they are still members of the party executive.
"My loyalty is to the people who voted me into parliament. The decision to expel me is unconstitutional," party vice president Mebelo Mutukwa said.
There has been little evidence of increasing social and economic unrest, as anticipated by the opposition.
Government has also managed to keep the local currency stable at around 1,230 per dollar over recent months, and saw inflation dip to its lowest annual level in eight years in 1996.
The new year has seen some industrial unrest, with university and council workers striking, but not on a scale anticipated by the opposition.

Western donors resumed talks with the government in April after a suspension of aid last year. According to diplomats, the donor states expressed some concerns about governance but did not specifically address the conduct of the 1996 elections.
Most countries offering assistance to Zambia now seem ready to resume normal aid flows after they hold a Consultative Group meeting in early July.
As one diplomat put it: "Western governments are likely to resume more or less normal aid flows this year if the government does not commit fresh violations."
